I am an economist and PhD candidate at the Faculty of Economics and Business,
Universitas Indonesia, and a civil servant in the Provincial Government of North
Sulawesi. My work has two strands that are usually kept apart: empirical
research on how communities absorb large shocks, and professional practice in
Indonesian public procurement. They share a single question — how public
resources and collective capacity are actually allocated when institutions are
under strain.

My research is in development, urban and regional, and spatial economics. The
dissertation asks what happens to social order and household behaviour after a
large physical shock, in a setting where formal insurance is thin and local
order is largely self-enforced. The first chapter combines twenty years of
Indonesia's Village Potential Survey with village-level earthquake intensity
surfaces and finds a pattern that neither of the standard stories predicts:
reported communal conflict falls after damage-level shaking, while theft rises
sharply on the same villages in the same waves. Not a general improvement in
security, then, but a change in the *kind* of violence a community can produce.
The second chapter turns to what households pay for religious and ceremonial
activity after a shock, using expenditure rather than stated belief to test
whether religion functions as informal insurance.

Building these papers has meant building the data infrastructure they rest on:
harmonising two decades of village boundary change onto a constant reference
year, converting seismic intensity rasters into village-level exposure, and
documenting the whole chain so that it can be reproduced. That work is
unglamorous and, in the Indonesian context, largely unavailable off the shelf.
It is also where most of the credibility of the results comes from.

Before graduate school I entered the civil service through IPDN, and my early
posts were in procurement — receiving completed work, then serving as a
procurement official, then as a commitment-making official responsible for
contracts. I have sat on provincial selection working groups and managed
construction, equipment, and consultancy contracts. Since 2018 I have worked
nationally as a certified procurement facilitator, and since 2020 as a
competency assessor, probity advisor, and member of the contract support team
of Indonesia's National Public Procurement Agency. I am also a certified
mediator and hold the World Bank's Certificate Professional in Public
Procurement.

That practical experience shaped what I find worth studying. Procurement is
where formal rules meet local discretion, and where the gap between what a
regulation requires and what an official can actually do is most visible. My
master's thesis used Indonesia's e-procurement records to ask whether more
bidders produce better outcomes; that work continues alongside the dissertation.

The longer-term agenda is to keep both strands running: rigorous empirical
economics on shocks, institutions, and local public goods in Indonesia, and a
serious contribution to the professionalisation of Indonesian public
procurement — including writing about procurement practice for practitioners,
not only for regulators.
